newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan's Fed-speak leaves spin doctors spinning.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan's Fed-speak leaves spin doctors spinning.

text.p: Wall Street -- it's up to you.

Most journalists covering Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's speech on Thursday night were daring enough to take a stand on whether the famously-cryptic Greenspan had implied the Fed will raise rates again to slow the booming economy.
Too bad they didn't agree.
The headlines in the nations major newspapers said it all -- literally.
"Greenspan Hints Fed Will Let Rates Stand" screamed The Washington Post's headline at the top of its business section.
However, USA Today wrote "Greenspan Hints at New Rate Increase" and "Greenspan Hints at Interest Rate Hike" said The Associated Press, as seen in New York's Daily News.
Even more bullish was the New York Post which printed in inch high capital letters, "GREENSPAN WARNS RATES MAY CLIMB".
Confused? So were some journalists who decided to stick to the facts -- at least in the headline.
The New York Times header topping its Business Day section read "Greenspan Defends Fed's Rate Policy".

Financiers' beloved The Wall Street Journal printed on its front-page business and finance column: "Fed Chief Greenspan made clear in a speech that he remains poised to boost rates further, while acknowledging that inflation seems in check."

Worse, this is not the first time media spin doctors have battled unsuccessfully with remarks from Greenspan, who recently proved that with two words -- "irrational exuberance" -- that he could send the financial markets plummetting.
Following a Greenspan speech on June 8, 1995, the headlines from The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal read as follows, respectively. See if you can spot the difference.
"Greenspan Sees Chance of Recession" and "Fed Chairman Doesn't See Recession on the Horizon".
On Friday, market players said they were relying on the Fed experts of Wall Street to interpret Greenspan's mixed bag of comments while having fun deciding which paper got it right.
"The Washinton Post came the closest," said Cary Leahey, senior economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc.
He said Greenspan's speech overall pointed to tighter monetary policy save one critical sentence saying that the Fed would need to act if growth fails to slow as expected.

"That's what the market is running on -- that sentence," he said. Early signs this quarter pointed to an economic slowdown from the torrid pace clocked in the first quarter, suggesting growth will taper and thus the Fed will not need to raise rates, the opposite of what Greenspan said.
Validating Leahey's argument was the early bullish performance of U.S. Treasury bonds and stocks, reportedly on hopes the Fed will leave monetary policy unchanged at its next May 20 meeting.
However, bonds pared losses and stocks turned negative by midday as the markets once again reassessed Greenspan's message.

Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc in New York said last night's speech was one of the strongest he's seen the Fed chief deliver, especially his adament defense of March's interest rate rise -- the first in more than two years.
However, multiple references to economic growth -- which has shown signs of slowing this quarter -- stole some of the the speech's thunder, he added.
"I can understand why we are getting conflicting headlines," he said.

When asked if the media would better serve its readers by not taking a stance, Moran replied, "There have been instances where the press has helped and instances where the press has muddied the water."
((-- Roanne Daniels, 212-859-1677))
